  of divorced households with that of married ones. Divorced households hold a
  fraction of the wealth of married households at every age, and the gap
  narrows but does not close once age, education and income are held

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 6, fig.height = 2.8, out.width = "100%",
                      fig.align = "center")

# The figure takes the style's own colours, so the chart belongs to its page.
pal <- docdesigner::designer_style(params$style)$color
accent <- pal$accent
muted  <- if (is.null(pal$muted)) "#666666" else pal$muted
textc  <- if (is.null(pal$text)) "#000000" else pal$text
# Grid lines are a faint wash of the rule colour: in a black-ink style the
# rule is black, and a full-strength grid competes with the data.
grid   <- grDevices::adjustcolor(if (is.null(pal$rule)) "#CCCCCC" else pal$rule, alpha.f = 0.3)

# The chart is drawn in the style's own body face, so its labels match the
# page. showtext loads the face from the style's font files; without it the
# chart falls back to a generic serif.
chart_family <- "serif"
if (requireNamespace("showtext", quietly = TRUE)) {
  chart_family <- tryCatch({
    spec <- docdesigner::designer_style(params$style)
    reg <- docdesigner:::dd_font_registry(spec)
    body <- spec$typography$body
    dir <- docdesigner:::dd_font_family_dir(body, reg, docdesigner:::dd_font_dirs(spec))
    path <- function(f) if (nzchar(dir)) file.path(dir, f) else system2("kpsewhich", f, stdout = TRUE)
    sysfonts::font_add("ddbody", regular = path(reg[[body]]$regular), bold = path(reg[[body]]$bold))
    showtext::showtext_opts(dpi = 300)
    knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.showtext = TRUE)
    "ddbody"
  }, error = function(e) "serif")
}

# One implicate of the public 2022 SCF (dev/make-specimen-data.R), in 2022
# dollars. Estimates use the survey weights; standard errors ignore the
# survey's design and its multiple imputation.
scf <- read.csv("scf2022-specimen.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
levels_m <- c("Married", "Living with partner", "Separated", "Divorced",
              "Widowed", "Never married")
scf$marital <- factor(scf$marital, levels = levels_m)

wmedian <- function(x, w) {
  o <- order(x); x <- x[o]; w <- w[o]
  x[which(cumsum(w) >= sum(w) / 2)[1]]
}
dollars <- function(x) paste0("$", formatC(round(x), format = "d", big.mark = ","))
f1 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1)
# Negative numbers take a true minus sign, not a hyphen.
f2 <- function(x) sub("^-", "−", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2))

by_status <- lapply(split(scf, scf$marital), function(g) c(
  share = 100 * sum(g$wgt) / sum(scf$wgt),
  median = wmedian(g$networth, g$wgt),
  mean = weighted.mean(g$networth, g$wgt),
  age = weighted.mean(g$age, g$wgt)))
med <- sapply(by_status, `[[`, "median")
overall <- wmedian(scf$networth, scf$wgt)
ratio <- med[["Divorced"]] / med[["Married"]]

# Net worth runs from large debts to billions; the inverse hyperbolic sine
# behaves like a logarithm but accepts zero and negative values.
scf$y <- asinh(scf$networth)
scf$college <- as.integer(scf$educ == "College degree")
scf$loginc <- log(pmax(scf$income, 1))
m1 <- lm(y ~ marital + age + I(age^2 / 100), data = scf, weights = wgt)
m2 <- update(m1, . ~ . + college + loginc)
b_div1 <- coef(m1)[["maritalDivorced"]]
b_div2 <- coef(m2)[["maritalDivorced"]]
explained <- round(100 * (1 - b_div2 / b_div1))
```

# Introduction

Marriage pools two incomes and two sets of assets, and divorce divides them,
often along with the costs of setting up a second household. Divorced people
have long been found to hold less wealth than married people, and the gap
grows with the years of marriage that precede it [@zagorsky2005]. This note
describes the gap in the most recent Survey of Consumer Finances, the Federal
Reserve's triennial survey of household balance sheets [@aladangady2023].

> Far better an approximate answer to the right question, which is often
> vague, than an exact answer to the wrong question.
>
> --- John W. Tukey [-@tukey1977]

# Data

The survey interviewed `r formatC(nrow(scf), big.mark = ",")` households in
2022, with weights that make them represent all American households. Net worth
is the value of a household's assets less its debts. Marital status is that of
the survey respondent: married, living with a partner, separated, divorced,
widowed or never married. Table 1 describes each group. The median household
held `r dollars(overall)`.

```{r stats}
tab1 <- data.frame(
  `Marital status` = levels_m,
  `Households (%)` = f1(sapply(by_status, `[[`, "share")),
  `Median net worth` = dollars(med),
  `Mean net worth` = dollars(sapply(by_status, `[[`, "mean")),
  `Mean age` = f1(sapply(by_status, `[[`, "age")),
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(tab1, format = "pipe", row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrr",
             caption = "Net worth by marital status, 2022")
```

# Results

The median divorced household held `r dollars(med[["Divorced"]])`, about
`r round(100 * ratio)` cents for every dollar held by the median married
household. Divorced respondents are older than married ones, so age alone
cannot account for the difference. Figure 1 compares the groups age by age:
the married hold more at every age, and the gap widens through middle age, as
married households' wealth climbs and divorced households' barely does.

```{r line, fig.cap = "Median net worth by age of respondent, 2022. Thousands of 2022 dollars."}
scf$agegrp <- cut(scf$age, c(17, 34, 44, 54, 64, 74, Inf),
                  labels = c("Under 35", "35-44", "45-54", "55-64", "65-74", "75+"))
groups <- c("Married", "Divorced", "Never married")
cols <- c(Married = textc, Divorced = accent, `Never married` = muted)
curves <- sapply(groups, function(m) sapply(levels(scf$agegrp), function(a) {
  g <- scf[scf$marital == m & scf$agegrp == a, ]
  wmedian(g$networth, g$wgt) / 1000
}))
par(mar = c(2.6, 3.8, 0.6, 0.6), mgp = c(2.4, 0.6, 0), tcl = -0.25,
    las = 1, bty = "n", col.axis = muted, col.lab = muted, cex.axis = 0.85,
    family = chart_family)
plot(NA, xlim = c(1, 6), ylim = c(0, max(curves) * 1.2), xaxt = "n",
     xlab = "", ylab = "Median net worth ($000s)")
abline(h = pretty(c(0, max(curves))), col = grid, lwd = 0.5)
axis(1, at = 1:6, labels = levels(scf$agegrp))
for (m in groups) {
  lines(1:6, curves[, m], col = cols[[m]], lwd = if (m == "Divorced") 2.2 else 1.4,
        lty = if (m == "Never married") 2 else 1)
  points(1:6, curves[, m], col = cols[[m]], pch = 16, cex = 0.6)
}
legend("topleft", legend = groups, col = cols, lwd = c(1.4, 2.2, 1.4), lty = c(1, 1, 2),
       bty = "n", cex = 0.8, text.col = muted, inset = c(0.04, 0), horiz = TRUE)
```

Table 2 reports two weighted regressions of net worth, on the inverse
hyperbolic sine scale, which behaves like a logarithm but accepts the zero and
negative net worth some households report. Holding age constant, the
coefficient on divorce is `r f2(b_div1)`. Adding education and income shrinks
it to `r f2(b_div2)`: differences in education and income account for about
`r explained`% of the gap, and the rest remains.

```{r reg}
stars <- function(p) ifelse(p < .001, "***", ifelse(p < .01, "**", ifelse(p < .05, "*", "")))
cell <- function(m, term) {
  co <- summary(m)$coefficients
  if (!term %in% rownames(co)) return(c("", ""))
  c(paste0(f2(co[term, 1]), stars(co[term, 4])), paste0("(", f2(co[term, 2]), ")"))
}
terms <- c(`maritalLiving with partner` = "Living with partner",
           maritalSeparated = "Separated", maritalDivorced = "Divorced",
           maritalWidowed = "Widowed", `maritalNever married` = "Never married",
           age = "Age", `I(age^2/100)` = "Age² / 100", college = "College degree",
           loginc = "Log income", `(Intercept)` = "Constant")
rows <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(terms), function(t) {
  a <- cell(m1, t); b <- cell(m2, t)
  data.frame(Term = c(terms[[t]], ""), `Model 1` = a, `Model 2` = b, check.names = FALSE)
}))
rows <- rbind(rows,
  data.frame(Term = c("Households", "R²"),
             `Model 1` = c(formatC(nobs(m1), big.mark = ","), f2(summary(m1)$r.squared)),
             `Model 2` = c(formatC(nobs(m2), big.mark = ","), f2(summary(m2)$r.squared)),
             check.names = FALSE))
knitr::kable(rows, format = "pipe", row.names = FALSE, align = "lrr",
             caption = "Weighted OLS models of net worth (inverse hyperbolic sine). Reference: married. Standard errors in parentheses; \\* p < .05, \\*\\* p < .01, \\*\\*\\* p < .001")
```

# Conclusion

In 2022, as in earlier work, divorced households held far less wealth than
married ones, and differences in age, education and income explain only part
of the gap. These data cannot say how much of it divorce causes and how much
reflects who divorces. That is the point of a specimen: the reader can attend
to how the page sets the argument rather than to the argument itself.
